title: Case L: Jack's noise-induced hearing loss
ask: Jack works in a very noisy open-plan office and has listened to loud music for a long time to drown it out. He now has trouble hearing and understanding. Which parts of the ear are damaged, and where are they? How does loud noise over time damage them, and how does that lead to deafness? What kind of deafness is this, and how does it compare with the other kind? (6 marks)
hook: Too loud, too long → hairs in the ORGAN OF CORTI snap off → no signal down nerve VIII → SENSORINEURAL, and permanent. The other kind (CONDUCTION) is a blockage before the inner ear: wax, glue ear, a hole in the eardrum.
steps: The damaged parts are the **hair cells** (the auditory **mechanoreceptors**) of the **organ of Corti**.
The organ of Corti sits on the **basilar membrane** in the **scala media (cochlear duct)** of the **cochlea**, in the **inner ear**.

Loud sound is a high-**amplitude** wave: the basilar membrane moves so hard that the hairs **bend against the tectorial membrane** until they **break off**. Continuous exposure to **85 dB** or more does this over time; **130 dB** or more does it at once.
Damaged hair cells cannot **transduce** vibration into **nerve impulses**, so no signal travels along the **vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)** to the **auditory cortex** in the temporal lobe.
Hair cells **do not grow back**, so noise-induced hearing loss is **permanent**.

This is **sensorineural deafness**: damage anywhere from the **cochlear hair cells** to the auditory cortex. It is usually **irreversible**; depending on where the damage is, a **cochlear implant** can help.

The other kind is **conduction deafness**: sound is **blocked before it reaches the inner ear** (outer or middle ear), e.g. **impacted earwax**, a **perforated eardrum** or a **middle-ear infection** (glue ear). It is often **reversible**.

short.hook: CORTI → SNAP → SILENT → SENSORINEURAL: where it breaks, how, what that does, what kind.

groups.q: Which parts are damaged, and where?

facts.t: They sit in the **organ of Corti**
on the **basilar membrane**, in the **cochlea** of the **inner ear**

groups.q: How does loud noise damage them?

facts.t: The hairs **bend against the tectorial membrane**
**85 dB** or more over time; **130 dB** at once
No **nerve impulses** go down **nerve VIII** to the brain
Hair cells **do not grow back**, so it is **permanent**

groups.q: What kind of deafness, and the other kind?

facts.t: **Sensorineural** deafness: damage from the cochlea to the brain
The other kind is **conduction**: sound is **blocked** in the outer or middle ear

traps: Hair cells of the SEMICIRCULAR CANALS are for balance. Her own NIHL question offers them as the wrong answer.
Noise-induced loss is SENSORINEURAL, even though the sound came in through a normal ear canal. Conduction means something BLOCKS the sound.
The case says 'be specific': name the organ of Corti AND where it sits (on the basilar membrane, scala media, cochlea, inner ear).

mcq.a: On the basilar membrane in the scala media
d: On the tympanic membrane in the middle ear
Inside the utricle of the vestibule
On the oval window beside the stapes
mcq.why: Her deck: the organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, the floor of the scala media (cochlear duct) inside the cochlea of the inner ear.

mcq.a: Their hairs bend so far they break off
d: Their hairs get coated in thick earwax
They fill up with fluid and burst open
They swell and block the oval window
mcq.why: Her slide: the hair cells in the cochlea bend so much that they break off. Earwax is a cause of conduction deafness, a different kind.

mcq.why: Her deck: continuous exposure to 85 dB or more can lead to sensorineural loss, and 130 dB or more causes it immediately.

mcq.q: Why do damaged receptor cells leave Jack deaf?
mcq.a: No vibration is turned into nerve impulses
d: Sound waves can no longer enter the ear
The ossicles stop amplifying the sound
The Eustachian tube cannot equalise pressure
mcq.why: Sound still reaches the cochlea, but without hair cells there is no transduction, so no impulse goes to the brain. The other three options describe conduction problems.

mcq.q: Which nerve would normally carry Jack's hearing signal to the brain?
mcq.why: The cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) carries hearing impulses on to the auditory cortex.

mcq.q: Why is noise-induced hearing loss permanent?
mcq.a: Lost hair cells do not grow back
d: The eardrum scars over for good
Earwax hardens and cannot be removed
The ossicles fuse into one bone
mcq.why: Hair cells that break off are not replaced, so the loss is permanent. Her NIHL question calls it permanent.

mcq.q: Which type of deafness is noise-induced hearing loss?
mcq.why: The damage is to the hair cells (a neural structure of the inner ear), so it is sensorineural. Her quiz key says the same.

mcq.q: Which of these would cause conduction deafness instead?
mcq.why: Conduction deafness blocks sound before the inner ear: earwax, a perforated eardrum, glue ear. The other three are sensorineural causes.

mcq.q: What makes conduction deafness different from sensorineural?
mcq.a: Sound is blocked before the inner ear
d: Hair cells can no longer make signals
The auditory cortex cannot process it
The cochlear nerve is cut or damaged
mcq.why: Conduction = the outer or middle ear stops sound reaching the cochlea, and it is often reversible. The other three are all sensorineural.

title: Glaucoma and cataracts
ask: Explain glaucoma and cataracts: which part of the eye each one affects, what goes wrong, and how it affects vision. (4 marks)
hook: GLAUCOMA = a PRESSURE problem: the drain (canal of Schlemm) blocks, fluid backs up, pressure crushes the retina and optic nerve. CATARACT = a CLARITY problem: the lens goes cloudy.
steps: **Glaucoma** involves the **aqueous humor**: normally the **ciliary body** makes it and the **canal of Schlemm** drains it at the same rate.
If the **canal of Schlemm is blocked** (or too much fluid is made), aqueous humor **builds up** in the **anterior** segment and **intraocular pressure rises**.
The raised pressure **compresses the retina** and its **blood supply** and damages the **optic nerve**, so vision is lost and it can end in **blindness**.
A **cataract** affects the **lens**: its **proteins denature**, so the lens turns **cloudy (opaque)** instead of transparent.
The cloudy lens stops light reaching the **retina** properly: vision becomes **blurred and yellowed**, with poor night vision and **glare** sensitivity. It is common with **age** and **diabetes**.
A cataract is treated with **surgery** that **replaces the lens**.

short.hook: GLAUCOMA = PRESSURE: the drain blocks and the nerve is crushed. CATARACT = a CLOUDY LENS.

groups.q: Glaucoma: where, what goes wrong, what it does

facts.t: **Glaucoma** is a problem with the **aqueous humor**
The **ciliary body** makes it; the **canal of Schlemm** drains it

groups.q: Cataract: where, what goes wrong, what it does

traps: Glaucoma = PRESSURE (aqueous humor, canal of Schlemm). Cataract = the LENS. Swapping them loses both marks.
The ciliary body MAKES aqueous humor; the canal of Schlemm DRAINS it.
In glaucoma the lens is fine: it is the retina and optic nerve that get damaged.

mcq.why: The ciliary body makes aqueous humor. The canal of Schlemm is the drain, which is what blocks in glaucoma.

mcq.why: The canal of Schlemm drains aqueous humor. The nasolacrimal duct drains tears, not aqueous humor.

mcq.why: A cataract is a cloudy lens. Her help board: cataract affects the clarity of the lens.

d: It is pushed back by high fluid pressure
It detaches from the suspensory ligaments
It loses its blood supply and dies off

mcq.q: Which symptom fits a cataract?
d: A sudden dark curtain over one eye
Ringing in both of the ears
mcq.why: Her Light & Seeing slide on cataract: reduced acuity, poor night vision, blurring and yellowing, sensitivity to glare.

mcq.q: How is a cataract treated?

mcq.why: Her Answers page shows cataract surgery, where the cloudy lens is replaced.

title: How hearing occurs
ask: Discuss how hearing occurs in humans, from the sound wave arriving at the ear to the sound being perceived. (4 marks)
hook: COLLECT (pinna) → VIBRATE (eardrum) → AMPLIFY (ossicles onto the oval window) → FLUID WAVES (perilymph → endolymph) → BEND (hair cells against the tectorial membrane) → IMPULSE (nerve VIII) → HEAR (auditory cortex, temporal lobe).
steps: **Outer ear**: the **pinna** collects sound waves and channels them along the **external auditory canal** to the **tympanic membrane**, which **vibrates**.
**Middle ear**: the vibration passes to the **ossicles** (**malleus → incus → stapes**), which **amplify** it onto the much smaller **oval window**.
**Inner ear**: the oval window vibrates the **perilymph** in the scala vestibuli and scala tympani, which passes the vibration to the **endolymph** in the **scala media** (cochlear duct).
The **basilar membrane** moves, and the **hair cells** of the **organ of Corti** **bend against the tectorial membrane**.
Bending the hairs is **transduction**: the hair cells (**mechanoreceptors**) turn the vibration into **nerve impulses**.
The impulses travel along the **cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)** to the **auditory cortex** in the **temporal lobe**, where the sound is heard.

short.hook: COLLECT → AMPLIFY → RIPPLE → BEND → FIRE → HEAR: outer ear, middle ear, inner ear, nerve, brain.

facts.t: The **pinna** collects sound; the **tympanic membrane** vibrates
The **ossicles** (**malleus → incus → stapes**) pass it on
The vibration moves the **perilymph**, then the **endolymph**
**Hair cells** of the **organ of Corti** **bend against the tectorial membrane**

groups.q: To the brain: fire and hear

facts.t: along **nerve VIII** to the **auditory cortex** in the **temporal lobe**

traps: It is the MIDDLE ear (the ossicles) that amplifies. Her student-marked feedback slips and says the inner ear amplifies; her deck (slide 11) says the middle ear.
The hair cells sit ON the basilar membrane and bend AGAINST the tectorial membrane.
The auditory cortex is in the TEMPORAL lobe; the occipital lobe is vision.

mcq.q: What does the pinna do?
mcq.a: Collects sound and funnels it inward
d: Amplifies sound onto the oval window
Equalises pressure in the middle ear
Turns sound waves into nerve impulses
mcq.why: The pinna collects sound like a satellite dish and channels it into the auditory canal. Amplifying is the ossicles' job.

mcq.q: Which part of the ear amplifies the vibrations?
mcq.a: The ossicles of the middle ear
d: The pinna of the outer ear
The cochlea of the inner ear
mcq.why: Her deck: the middle ear amplifies, passing vibration from the large eardrum to the small oval window.

mcq.q: In what order do the ossicles pass on the vibration?
mcq.why: The malleus touches the eardrum, the incus sits in the middle, and the stapes fits into the oval window.

mcq.q: Which fluid does the oval window set moving first?
mcq.why: The oval window vibrates the perilymph in the scala vestibuli and tympani; that passes the vibration on to the endolymph of the scala media.

mcq.why: The hair cells sit on the basilar membrane with their hairs in the gel-like tectorial membrane. Bending against it fires them.

mcq.why: They respond to bending (a mechanical stimulus). Her Answers page: the inner ear contains mechanoreceptors.

mcq.why: Her deck: impulses are projected to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

mcq.why: Nerve VIII has a cochlear branch (hearing) and a vestibular branch (balance).

title: The three regions of the ear
ask: What are the three regions of the ear? Describe their structures and functions. (4.5 marks)
hook: OUTER collects (pinna, canal, eardrum). MIDDLE amplifies (three bones, a pressure tube, two damping muscles). INNER turns it into signals: cochlea = hearing, vestibular apparatus = balance.
steps: **Outer (external) ear**: the **pinna**, the **external auditory canal** (with glands making **cerumen**, earwax) and the **tympanic membrane**. It **collects** sound and directs it onto the eardrum; the pinna also helps **locate** sound (above or below).

**Middle ear**: an air-filled cavity in the **temporal bone** holding the **ossicles** (malleus, incus, stapes). It **amplifies** sound, passing it from the large eardrum to the small **oval window**.

The middle ear also has the **Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube** to the nasopharynx, which **equalises pressure**, and two small **muscles** (tensor tympani and stapedius) that **dampen loud sounds**.
**Inner ear**: the **bony labyrinth** in the temporal bone, filled with **perilymph**, holding the **membranous labyrinth**, filled with **endolymph**.
Inner ear part 1: the **cochlea**, for **hearing**; its **organ of Corti** turns sound vibration into nerve impulses.
Inner ear part 2: the **vestibular apparatus** (the **vestibule** and the **semicircular canals**), for **equilibrium (balance)**.

short.hook: OUTER collects, MIDDLE amplifies, INNER senses: the cochlea hears, the vestibular apparatus balances.

facts.t: It **collects** sound onto the eardrum and helps **locate** it
Air-filled, in the **temporal bone**; holds the **ossicles**

traps: Only the INNER ear does balance. The outer and middle ear are for hearing only.
The Eustachian tube equalises PRESSURE (the ear 'pops'); it does not carry sound.
PERIlymph is in the bony labyrinth, around the outside; ENDOlymph is inside the membranous labyrinth.
her: what are the three regions of the ear

mcq.why: The outer ear is the pinna, the canal and the eardrum. The ossicles are middle ear; the cochlea and vestibular apparatus are inner ear.

mcq.q: What is cerumen?
mcq.a: Earwax made in the auditory canal

mcq.why: Cerumen is earwax, from the wax glands of the external auditory canal.

mcq.q: What is the main job of the middle ear?
mcq.a: Amplify sound onto the oval window
mcq.why: Her deck: the middle ear amplifies the intensity of sound, from the large tympanic membrane to the small oval window.

mcq.q: What does the Eustachian tube do?
mcq.why: It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx so the pressure on both sides of the eardrum matches. That is why ears pop.

mcq.why: Endo = inside: endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth. Perilymph surrounds it in the bony labyrinth.

mcq.q: Which part of the inner ear is for hearing?
mcq.why: The cochlea (with the organ of Corti) is for hearing. The utricle, saccule and ampullae are balance organs.

mcq.q: Which region of the ear handles balance as well as hearing?
mcq.why: Her deck: the external and middle ear are involved with hearing only; the internal ear does both hearing and equilibrium.

title: The three layers of the eye
ask: What are the three layers (tunics) of the eye? Give their structures and functions. (4.5 marks)
hook: Outside in: TOUGH COAT (sclera + cornea) → BLOOD COAT (choroid, ciliary body, iris) → SEEING COAT (retina: pigment layer + rods/cones → bipolar → ganglion → optic nerve).
steps: **Fibrous tunic** (outer): the white **sclera** (**protects** the eye and **anchors** the extrinsic muscles) and the transparent **cornea** (lets light in and does about **80% of the refraction**).
**Vascular tunic (uvea)** (middle), part 1: the **choroid**, pigmented and **rich in blood vessels**; it **nourishes** the other layers and stops light scattering.
Vascular tunic, part 2: the **ciliary body** (ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments) **holds the lens and changes its shape**, and its processes **make aqueous humor**.
Vascular tunic, part 3: the **iris**, whose circular and radial muscles **control pupil size** and so how much light enters.
**Neural tunic** (inner) = the **retina**. Its outer **pigmented layer** **absorbs light** and stops it scattering.

The retina's inner **neural layer** has three layers of neurons: **photoreceptors (rods and cones)** → **bipolar cells** → **ganglion cells**, whose axons leave as the **optic nerve (II)**. The photoreceptors **turn light into nerve impulses**.

short.hook: Outside in: TOUGH COAT (sclera, cornea) → BLOOD COAT (choroid, ciliary body, iris) → SEEING COAT (retina).

facts.t: **Cornea**: clear, does about **80% of the refraction**
**Ciliary body**: **holds the lens and changes its shape**
Their axons leave as the **optic nerve (II)**

traps: The CORNEA, not the lens, does most of the refraction (about 80%).
The choroid is part of the VASCULAR (middle) tunic, not the retina.
Rods and cones are in the NEURAL layer; the pigmented layer only absorbs light.
her: what are the three layers of the eye
src: Her 2022 Eyes deck slides 7-14 (three tunics; sclera protects and anchors muscles; cornea refracts 80%; choroid supplies nutrients and prevents scattering; ciliary body; iris muscles; retina pigmented layer and neural layer: photoreceptors, bipolar, ganglion cells, optic nerve II); slide 15 (ciliary body produces aqueous humor).

mcq.q: Which part of the outer tunic lets light in and does most of the refraction?
mcq.why: Her deck: the cornea is the window that lets light in and refracts about 80% of it. The lens does the rest.

mcq.q: What does the sclera do?
mcq.a: Protects the eye and anchors its muscles
mcq.why: The sclera is the tough white coat: it protects the eye and anchors the extrinsic eye muscles.

mcq.q: Which layer of the eye is rich in blood vessels and nourishes the others?
mcq.why: The choroid is the highly vascular, pigmented part of the middle tunic.

mcq.q: Which structure changes the shape of the lens?
mcq.why: The ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments of the ciliary body hold the lens and change its shape.

mcq.q: What does the iris control?
mcq.why: The iris's circular and radial muscles make the pupil smaller or larger, controlling how much light enters.

mcq.q: What does the retina's pigmented layer do?
mcq.a: Absorbs light so it does not scatter
d: Makes aqueous humor for the lens
Carries impulses to the optic nerve
mcq.why: The pigmented layer absorbs stray light. Turning light into impulses is the photoreceptors' job in the neural layer.

mcq.q: Which cells of the retina turn light into nerve impulses?
mcq.why: The photoreceptors (rods and cones) transduce light; bipolar and ganglion cells pass the signal on.

mcq.q: Whose axons leave the eye as the optic nerve?
mcq.why: Her deck: the axons of the ganglion cells leave the eye as the optic nerve (II).

title: Near vision: the three changes
ask: What changes occur in the eye to allow near vision? How is this undone for distant vision? (3 marks)
hook: Reading a book close up = BULGE, SHRINK, CROSS: the lens bulges, the pupils shrink, the eyes cross inwards. Look out the window and all three undo.
steps: The **lens bulges (gets rounder)**: the **ciliary muscle contracts**, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the elastic lens recoils, so it bends light more. This is **accommodation** of the lens.
The **pupils constrict**: the **circular (sphincter) muscles** of the iris contract.
The eyes **converge**: both eyeballs **rotate medially (turn inwards)** toward the near object.
For distant vision all three are undone: the **ciliary muscle relaxes**, the **lens flattens**, the **pupils dilate** and the eyes look straight ahead.
Light from a near object arrives as **diverging rays**; light from more than **6 m** away arrives as **parallel rays**. Near rays need more bending to focus on the **retina**.

short.hook: Near = BULGE, SHRINK, CROSS. Far = all three undo.

facts.t: Near light arrives **diverging**; from over **6 m** it is **parallel**

traps: For near vision the pupil CONSTRICTS. Her student-marked feedback says it dilates; her own quiz key ('the pupil dilates' is NOT typical) and both her decks say constricts. Write constricts.
The ciliary muscle CONTRACTS to make the lens BULGE. Her True/False trap says it contracts to flatten the lens (false).
Her Light & Seeing slide 10 slips and calls the lens 'biconcave'; it is BICONVEX (her slide 12 and the Eyes deck).
her: what changes occur in the eye to allow for near vision
src: Her 'Answers for 12' page Q7 (Patton's 3 changes: lens bulges, eyes converge, pupils constrict); 2022 Eyes deck slides 17-18 (near: ciliary muscle contracts, lens bulges, pupil constricts, convergence; far: ciliary muscle relaxes, lens flatter, pupils dilate, over 6 m = parallel rays); 2026 Light & Seeing deck slide 13 (the distant vs close vision table); her Special Senses quiz keys.

mcq.q: What is accommodation of the lens?
mcq.why: Accommodation is the lens changing shape (rounder for near, flatter for far) to focus the image on the retina.

mcq.why: Her decks and her quiz key: the pupil constricts for near vision. 'Dilates' is the wrong option in her question.

mcq.why: Her deck: constriction of the pupil = contraction of the circular (sphincter) muscles; dilation = the radial muscles.

mcq.q: What do the eyeballs do to view a near object?
mcq.why: Convergence is the medial rotation of both eyeballs toward the near object.

mcq.q: When you look far away, what happens to the lens?
mcq.a: It flattens as the ciliary muscle relaxes
d: It bulges as the ciliary muscle contracts
It flattens as the ciliary muscle contracts
It bulges as the iris muscle contracts
mcq.why: For distance, the ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens is pulled thin and flat.

mcq.q: How do light rays from a near object reach the eye?
mcq.why: Near rays spread out (diverge), so the lens must bend them more. Rays from over 6 m away are near parallel.

title: Myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism
ask: Explain how myopia, emmetropia and hyperopia differ and how each error is corrected. What is astigmatism? (5 marks)
hook: MYopia = MY world is up close (short-sighted): focus falls SHORT, in front of the retina → CONCAVE lens pushes it back. HYPERopia = long-sighted: focus overshoots, behind the retina → CONVEX lens pulls it forward.
steps: **Emmetropia** is normal vision: parallel light rays are **focused on the retina**.

**Myopia** (short-sighted): light from distant objects focuses **in front of the retina**, usually because the eyeball is **too long** (the eye over-focuses). Near things are clear; far things are blurred.
Myopia is corrected with a **concave (biconcave) lens**, which **diverges** (scatters) the light and moves the focus **back onto the retina**.
**Hyperopia** (long-sighted): light from near objects focuses **behind the retina**, usually because the eyeball is **too short** (the eye under-focuses). Far things are clearer than near.
Hyperopia is corrected with a **convex (biconvex) lens**, which **converges** the light and moves the focus **forward onto the retina**.

**Astigmatism**: the **cornea or lens is curved unevenly** (more in one direction), so light focuses at **several points** and vision is blurred at **all distances**. It is corrected with glasses or contacts, or laser surgery (LASIK).

short.hook: MY-opia: MY world is close, focus falls SHORT → conCAVE. HYPER-opia: focus overshoots → conVEX.

facts.t: **Myopia**: distant light focuses **in front of the retina**
The eyeball is **too long**; far things blur
Fixed with a **concave** lens, which **diverges** the light
The eyeball is **too short**; near things blur
Fixed with a **convex** lens, which **converges** the light
The **cornea or lens is curved unevenly**
Light focuses at **several points**: blurred at **all distances**
Fixed with glasses, contacts or **laser surgery**

traps: Myopia = SHORT-sighted = CONCAVE lens. Hyperopia = LONG-sighted = CONVEX lens. Swapping the lenses is the commonest slip.
Say WHERE the image falls (in front of or behind the retina). That is the mark, not just 'blurry'.
Astigmatism does not depend on how far away you look (her feedback).
her: explain how myopia emmetropia and hyperopia are different
src: Her 2022 Eyes deck slide 23 (emmetropic, myopic, hyperopic eye); 2026 Light & Seeing deck slide 12 (concave lens diverges, convex converges), slide 14 (hyperopia: eyeball too short, convex lens; myopia: eyeball too long, concave lens), slides 16 and 21-23 (astigmatism, what each person sees); her student-marked SAQ answers on refraction errors, astigmatism and corrective lenses.

mcq.q: In emmetropia, where do parallel light rays focus?
mcq.why: Emmetropia is the normal eye: parallel rays focus exactly on the retina.

mcq.q: In myopia, where does light from a distant object focus?
mcq.why: The myopic eye over-focuses, so the image falls short, in front of the retina.

mcq.q: What shape problem usually causes short-sightedness?
mcq.a: An eyeball that is too long
d: An eyeball that is too short
A cornea that is too flat
A lens that is too thin
mcq.why: Her deck: myopic eye, eyeball too long. Hyperopia is the too-short eyeball.

mcq.q: Which lens corrects short-sightedness?
mcq.why: A concave lens spreads the light out so the focus moves back onto the retina.

mcq.q: What does a long-sighted person struggle with most?
mcq.why: In hyperopia near objects focus behind the retina, so close work blurs while distance is clearer.

mcq.q: Which lens corrects hyperopia?
mcq.why: A convex lens bends the light inwards so the focus moves forward onto the retina.

mcq.q: What causes astigmatism?
mcq.a: Uneven curve of the cornea or lens
d: A cloudy lens after protein damage
mcq.why: Her deck: the front of the eye or the lens is curved differently in one direction than the other. The distractors are cataract, glaucoma and colour blindness.

title: Static vs dynamic equilibrium
ask: What is the difference between static and dynamic equilibrium? How and where is each detected? (4 marks)
hook: STATIC = gravity and straight lines (tilt, lift): the VESTIBULE's maculae, where ear stones slide. DYNAMIC = spinning: the SEMICIRCULAR CANALS' cristae, where fluid swings a gel cap.
steps: Both are sensed in the **vestibular apparatus** of the **inner ear** by **hair cells** (mechanoreceptors), which fire when **fluid (endolymph)** or a gel mass moves and **bends their hairs**.
**Static equilibrium** is the position of the head **in response to gravity** and **straight-line movement**: tilting the head, moving forwards or backwards, an accelerating lift.

Static equilibrium is detected by the **maculae** in the **utricle and saccule** (the **vestibule**): hairs embedded in a jelly **otolith membrane** studded with tiny stones (**otoliths**) that slide when the head tilts.
**Dynamic equilibrium** is balance while the head is **rotating** (angular movement), such as turning or spinning.
Dynamic equilibrium is detected by the **crista ampullaris** in the **ampulla** of each **semicircular canal**: rotation moves the endolymph, which swings the gel **cupula** and bends the hairs.
Impulses travel in the **vestibular branch of nerve VIII** to the **brain stem** and **cerebellum** (and the cortex). Signals that fire with no real movement cause **vertigo**.

short.hook: STATIC = GRAVITY and straight lines: the VESTIBULE, stones slide. DYNAMIC = SPINNING: the CANALS, a gel cap swings.

facts.t: **Hair cells** in the **vestibular apparatus** fire when their hairs bend
Signals go along **nerve VIII** to the **cerebellum**
**Static**: head position **in response to gravity** and **straight-line movement**
Detected by the **maculae** in the **utricle and saccule**
**Otoliths** (ear stones) slide when the head tilts
Detected by the **crista ampullaris** in each **semicircular canal**
Rotation swings the gel **cupula**, bending the hairs

traps: Static = the VESTIBULE (utricle, saccule, maculae, otoliths). Dynamic = the SEMICIRCULAR CANALS (ampulla, crista, cupula). Swapping them loses both marks.
Static does not mean 'no movement at all': it includes straight-line movement like a lift. Dynamic means ROTATION.
The cochlea is for hearing, not balance.
her: what is the different between the static and dynamic equilibrium
src: Her 2026 Hearing & Equilibrium deck slides 25-30 (vestibule: saccule, utricle, maculae, otolith membrane with otoliths; semicircular canals: ampulla, crista ampullaris, cupula, rotational movement; vestibular branch of VIII to the brain stem and cerebellum); her 'Answers for 12' page Q2 (the static vs dynamic table) and Q4 (mechanoreceptors).

mcq.q: What kind of receptors sense balance in the inner ear?
d: Free nerve endings, which sense pain
mcq.why: Her Answers page: the inner ear contains mechanoreceptors with hairs that fire when the hairs bend.

mcq.q: Standing in a lift that suddenly starts to rise mainly uses which sense?
mcq.why: Her deck gives the sudden acceleration of a lift as a static equilibrium example: straight-line movement, not rotation.

mcq.q: Where are the receptors for static equilibrium?
mcq.a: Maculae of the utricle and saccule
d: Organ of Corti in the cochlea
Hair cells on the tympanic membrane
mcq.why: Static equilibrium uses the maculae in the vestibule (utricle and saccule).

mcq.q: What are otoliths?
mcq.a: Tiny stones on the macula's gel
d: Small bones of the middle ear
Gel caps over the cochlear hairs
mcq.why: Otoliths ('ear stones') sit on the jelly-like otolith membrane; they slide when the head tilts and bend the hairs below.

mcq.q: Spinning around on an office chair mainly stimulates...
mcq.why: Rotation of the head is dynamic equilibrium, sensed in the semicircular canals.

mcq.q: Which structure detects rotation of the head?
mcq.a: Crista ampullaris of the semicircular canals
d: Macula of the utricle in the vestibule
Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane
mcq.why: Each semicircular canal has a swollen ampulla holding the crista ampullaris, the dynamic equilibrium receptor.

mcq.q: Where do balance impulses from nerve VIII mainly travel?
mcq.why: Her deck: the vestibular branch of VIII runs mainly to the brain stem and cerebellum, and also to the cortex.

title: Waves: light and sound
ask: Explain amplitude, wavelength and frequency and how we experience each. Compare light and sound waves, and explain the difference between reflection and refraction of light. (4 marks)
hook: Amplitude = how TALL (loud / bright). Wavelength = peak to peak (colour). Frequency = how MANY per second (pitch); more waves = shorter waves. Reflection BOUNCES, refraction BENDS.
steps: **Amplitude** is the **height** of the wave (how far it moves from rest). We experience it as **loudness** in sound (measured in **decibels, dB**) and **brightness** in light.
**Wavelength** is the distance from **one peak to the next**. In light it decides the **colour** we see (visible light is measured in **nm**).

**Frequency** is the number of waves passing **per second**, in **hertz (Hz)**. As frequency goes **up**, wavelength goes **down**. In sound we hear frequency as **pitch** (humans hear about **20-20,000 Hz**).

**Light** is **electromagnetic** and needs **no medium** (it can cross a vacuum). **Sound** is a **mechanical pressure wave** of compressions and rarefactions and **needs a medium** (gas, liquid or solid).
**Reflection**: light **bounces back** off a flat, opaque surface, e.g. a **mirror**. A coloured object reflects only its own wavelengths and absorbs the rest.

**Refraction**: light **bends** when it passes into a medium of **different density**, because it **slows down** there, e.g. a **rainbow** in raindrops, and the **cornea and lens** focusing light on the retina.

short.hook: TALL = loud or bright. PEAK TO PEAK = colour. HOW MANY = pitch. Reflection BOUNCES, refraction BENDS.

facts.t: **Refraction**: light **bends** as it **slows down** in a different density
e.g. a **rainbow**, or the **cornea and lens** focusing light

traps: Loudness = AMPLITUDE; pitch = FREQUENCY. Her quizzes swap them to catch you.
Higher frequency = SHORTER wavelength (her slide fills in the blank: decreases).
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; light can.

mcq.q: Which wave property do we hear as loudness?
mcq.why: Her deck: loudness is the interpretation of wave amplitude, measured in decibels.

mcq.q: What is a wavelength?
mcq.a: Distance from one peak to the next
d: Height of the wave from rest
Speed of the wave in air
mcq.why: Wavelength is peak to peak. Height is amplitude; waves per second is frequency.

mcq.q: In visible light, what does the wavelength decide?
mcq.why: Different wavelengths of visible light are different colours. Brightness is amplitude.

mcq.q: As frequency increases, the wavelength...
mcq.why: Her slide: as frequency increases, wavelength decreases. More waves fit into each second only if each one is shorter.

mcq.q: We hear the frequency of a sound as its...
mcq.why: Her deck: pitch is the perception of different frequencies. Loudness (volume) is amplitude.

mcq.q: Which statement about light and sound is true?
mcq.a: Light can cross a vacuum; sound cannot
d: Sound can cross a vacuum; light cannot
Both need air to travel through
mcq.why: Light is electromagnetic and needs no medium. Sound is a pressure wave and needs particles to push through.

mcq.q: Light bouncing back off a mirror is called...
mcq.why: Reflection is light bouncing back off a flat, opaque surface.

mcq.q: Why does light bend as it passes into water?
mcq.a: It slows in the denser medium
d: It speeds up in the denser medium
It is absorbed by the water
mcq.why: Her slide: light is refracted when it travels from one medium to another, because it travels slower in an optically denser medium.
